overview.text: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun and one of the solar system’s two ice giants, with an interior rich in water, ammonia, and methane “ices”—unlike the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn. Its atmosphere is mostly hydrogen and helium, with methane that absorbs red light and gives the planet its blue-green color. Uranus’s extreme axial tilt—about 98 degrees—makes it rotate almost on its side, producing unusually long seasons. Faint rings and dozens of moons surround the planet. Its distinctive tilt, rings, and moon system make Uranus an important world for understanding the outer solar system, but it has been visited up close by only one spacecraft: Voyager 2.

key_facts.text: Uranus was discovered by William Herschel in 1781 and was the first planet discovered with the aid of a telescope.
Its axis is tilted about 98 degrees relative to its orbit; the cause is uncertain, though a major collision is one proposed explanation.
Methane in Uranus’s atmosphere absorbs red light, helping give the planet its blue-green appearance.
Uranus has 13 faint rings: nine inner rings and two outer rings, alongside narrow ring structures described by NASA.
Voyager 2 made the only spacecraft close approach to Uranus, in January 1986.
Uranus’s moons include five major ones—Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon—and are named mainly for characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.
